newsitem.title: HONG KONG: IPO VIEW-GITIC saga seen positive in long run.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW-GITIC saga seen positive in long run.

text.p: Hong Kong's initial public offer (IPO) market needs to elimintate some grey areas following the confusion over GITIC Enteprises Ltd in order to facilitate future listings of red-chips and H-shares, analysts said.
Rumours spread in the market on Tuesday that red-chip GITIC Enterprises' IPO had hit a snag that could possibly lead to a withdrawal of the listing.
The building materials company is indirectly controlled by Guangdong International Trust and Investment Corp (GITIC), the provincial government's investment arm.
Brokers said they heard GITIC Enterprises may not have obtained all the necessary approval from the China Securities Regulation Commission (CSRC), China's securities watchdog.
The Guangdong provincial government-backed GITIC Enterprises said on Wednesday that its Hong Kong IPO and listing plan would proceed on schedule. But it did not clarify the rumours.

Analysts said the saga pointed to grey areas in listing procedures including insufficient communications between Hong Kong and mainland regulators, and concern over the flexibility of future asset injections into listed firms by China-based parents.
"It was a bit confusing trying to tell what kind of approval should be obtained from which authorities," said an analyst at a local brokerage.
Red-chips are China-related companies, often with parents based on the mainland, while H-shares are Hong Kong-listed shares of China-incorporated enterprises.

Analysts said investors could take a more cautious attitude towards red-chips and China-plays near term, but added that the GITIC saga was good for the IPO market in the long run as it should encourage solutions to underlying problems.
"To bring out the issues is good in the long run as it has to be sorted out sooner or later," said Eugene Law, director at Lippo Securities.

"Many are expecting a compromise or agreement on what kinds of things will get Chinese approval and what will not," he said. "I think the most important is for everybody to know the rules of the game."
Analysts generally agreed that problems could be solved through better communications and better understanding between the two regulators.

"It (the saga) can encourage them to establish a more systematic and efficienct way of communicating, and this in turn will smooth the operation of the market," said Patrick Cheng, corporate finance director at HSBC Investment Bank.
A spokesman at the Hong Kong stock exchange said: "We are having regular meetings with CSRC every three months to discuss some issues of common concern."
The spokesman added that both local and overseas companies seeking listings in Hong Kong should observe and fulfil the laws and regulations in their respective countries.
Corporate finance sources said issuers and merchant banks could take extra precautions in obtaining the necessary approval from relevant authorities when they prepare a listing in future.
But analysts generally do not expect the saga to delay any coming IPO plans.
"I see (the saga having) a neutral impact on the GITIC IPO in view of its strong subscription," Cheng added.
GITIC Enterprises' much anticipated IPO is likely to become one of Hong Kong's most popular ever, with market sources saying they expect the issue to be subscribed by between 900 and 1,000 times.
Dealing in the shares is due to begin on March 26.
